entities.summary:
Ercole Rangoni (1491–1527) was an influential Italian cardinal during the tumultuous early decades of the 16th century, a period marked by the high Renaissance, escalating Italian Wars, and the nascent Protestant Reformation. Elevated to cardinal by Pope Leo X in 1517, he served the Holy See for a decade, navigating the complex political and religious landscape of the Papal States and beyond. A scion of the noble Rangoni family of Modena, his career exemplified the intertwining of aristocratic power, ecclesiastical authority, and cultural patronage characteristic of the Italian Renaissance papacy, connecting him directly to the Medici popes and the geopolitical struggles for control of the Italian peninsula.

Rangoni's cardinalate began on July 1, 1517, when he was created Cardinal-Deacon of Santa Agata alla Suburra, later transferring to Santa Maria in Cosmedin. He held the legateship of Bologna from 1517 to 1520, a crucial administrative and diplomatic post that placed him at the heart of papal temporal power in northern Italy. A trusted advisor to Pope Leo X, Rangoni was part of the inner circle that grappled with the initial challenges posed by Martin Luther's theses. Following Leo X's death, he participated in the 1521–22 conclave that elected Pope Adrian VI and the 1523 conclave that elevated Giulio de' Medici to the papacy as Clement VII, demonstrating his continued relevance within the Curia.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ercole Rangoni played a significant regional role as a cardinal and papal legate during a volatile period of Italian history, directly influencing papal politics and contributing to Renaissance cultural patronage. His career and death reflect the complex interplay of power, religion, and culture that defined the early 16th century.
